title: Is Carl Hendrick Right about Reading?
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos, an elementary reading specialist, takes Carl Hendrick's essay on the humility of deep reading and turns it on the long-running reading wars. She asks whether the opponents of instruction built around orthographic mapping display the very vices Hendrick names: feeding on the familiar, judging before understanding, and clinging to predetermined ideas. She concedes the move is arbitrary and asserts rather than proves that her side is right, but argues the decades-long refusal to accept what reading research implies for foundational skills is a failure of intellectual humility. She holds up Anna Geiger's move from Balanced Literacy to Structured Literacy as the model of that humility. She closes by tying Hendrick's case for deep reading back to the first and second graders who cannot yet decode and so never reach the worlds that reading opens.
points: Janetos borrows Hendrick's list of intellectual vices (hubris, brittleness, judging before understanding) and applies it to opponents of structured, orthographic-mapping-based phonics instruction.
She openly admits the application is a leap of logic that asserts rather than proves her position, which keeps the piece honest as a rhetorical exercise.
Anna Geiger's account of researching Hanford's claims and discovering she was wrong is offered as the template for changing one's mind in the reading debate.
Her central stake is equity: children who cannot decode are shut out of the deep reading Hendrick celebrates, so the fundamentals are a moral obligation.
quotes: Are the opponents of a shift in foundational reading skills instruction that prioritizes orthographic mapping a good example of the problematic attitudes and attributes explored in “The Humility of the Page”?

Reading has become less an encounter with otherness than a sort of hyper-consumption of sameness where we feed on the familiar until the foreign becomes unpalatable . . . To inhabit unfamiliar minds, to wrestle with conflicting ideas, to sit with discomfort rather than resolve it prematurely got me out of myself and fostered a kind of humility, a recognition that my instincts were not final
To give ourselves to a complex text is to practice the patience we need for one another. It is a rehearsal in understanding before judging, listening before reacting

To what end, then? To detail the idiocy of the debate because there is no real debate unless it exhibits all the qualities Carl Hendrick explores. If there is no reckoning with the decades-long failure to accept the instructional implications of reading research from those who continue to match mistaken ideas with recommended practice, then this closed view of the reading world will remain the dominant one in many of our schools to the detriment of the children we teach.

But I never got very far: as it turned out, I didn’t know as much about how reading works as I thought I did. I began looking into the research myself. It didn’t take long to discover that Hanford was right.

For my intervention students who can’t read, they would gladly strike this deal: If we can’t have the full reading experience, then at least provide us with the fundamentals for decoding words so that we can benefit from their utility if not their ability to unify humanity.

Unintentionally, he has also reminded me that we continue to betray students who will be forgotten through no fault of their own. We are choosing to leave them behind because we are blind to the barriers we’ve constructed that have barred them from stepping over the threshold into literacy.
